metadata.title: Expecting less in hard times: How the state of the economy influences students’ educational expectations

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA microdata (students aged 15–16) merged with OECD macroeconomic indicators (GDP growth) and estimates within-country fixed-effects regressions with year fixed effects. The manuscript describes PISA’s two-stage sampling (schools sampled probabilistically; up to 35 students randomly selected per school) and clusters standard errors at the school level, but it does not report applying PISA sampling weights or replicate weights in the estimation. Because the analysis is regression-based (not ML with explicit survey-weight support), the paper does not specify a weight variable (e.g., TOTWGT/W_FSTUWT) to use from the OECD PISA database. Analysts using the OECD PISA data should consult the PISA technical documentation for the appropriate student sampling weights and replicate weights; however, this paper’s results cannot be assumed to be population-representative unless weights were applied (not stated).

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables are educational expectations converted to expected years of schooling (from ISCED-based responses), expected occupational status at age 30, and several binary behavioural indicators (homework/out-of-school lessons and arriving late). These outcomes are not described as being derived from PISA plausible values (PV-based achievement scores are used only as covariates, not as PV-based dependent variables). The paper also does not report a specific missing-data strategy for the analytic sample beyond including indicators for missing covariates, so a full missing-data handling method is not documented.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Uses PISA student observations from 38 OECD countries across four PISA waves where educational expectations are measured (2003, 2009, 2015, 2018). The analysis merges student records with annual real GDP growth from the year prior to PISA administration (GDP growth years 2002, 2008, 2014, 2017) and estimates within-country fixed-effects models. The estimation sample is restricted to the 38 OECD countries listed in Appendix Table A1, and models include indicators for missing values on covariates (rather than deleting cases), with reading achievement standardized within country-year. The paper does not specify additional exclusions (e.g., grade bands beyond PISA’s 15-year-old target, or specific item-completion requirements) beyond the country restriction and the availability of the expectation/behaviour measures in the specified PISA waves.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2003/2009/2015/2018 (age 15–16) Educational expectations (expected years of schooling, ISCED-based)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Fixed-effects regression (country + year FE), clustered SE at school level. GDP growth (%): 0.046 years per 1 pp increase (p < 0.001). Standardised GDP growth: +0.191 years per 1 SD increase (p < 0.001). GDP growth quintiles (ref Quintile 1): Quintile 4 = +0.335 years (p < 0.001); Quintile 5 = +0.388 years (p < 0.001). N = 885,247 across 38 countries.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2003/2009/2015/2018 data on students’ expected years of education, the study leveraged GDP growth (macro conditions) alongside tertiary-educated parent status, reading achievement, sex, and school location to model within-country changes in expectations, finding that higher GDP growth is associated with higher educational expectations and contracting economies reduce them (e.g., +0.191 years per 1 SD higher GDP growth; quintile 5 vs quintile 1: +0.388 years). This indicates that macroeconomic conditions can shift students’ schooling plans, suggesting that education systems may need to proactively support expectation formation during economic downturns, especially for lower-achieving and non-metropolitan students, though the estimates are correlational rather than causal.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2003/2009/2015/2018 (age 15–16) Educational expectations (expected years of schooling, ISCED-based)
main_findings.target_variable: Expected occupational status at age 30 (expected returns to education)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Fixed-effects regression (country + year FE), clustered SE at school level. Expected years of education: 3.805 (p < 0.001). Interaction (GDP growth standardised by country × expected years of education): 0.712 (p < 0.001). Implied association: when GDP growth is 1 SD below average, expected returns association = 3.140; when 1 SD above average, = 4.564. N = 519,600 across 38 countries.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2003/2009/2015/2018 data on expected years of education and expected occupational status at age 30, the study leveraged expected years of education and GDP growth (plus reading achievement, tertiary-educated parent status, and school location) to estimate how perceived returns vary with the economy, finding that the education-to-occupation association strengthens during economic expansion (interaction = 0.712, p < 0.001). This indicates that students’ educational expectations may fall in downturns partly because they anticipate lower returns to additional schooling, implying that policy responses during recessions should include credible information and support mechanisms that sustain perceived benefits of post-compulsory education, while noting the paper’s association-based identification assumptions.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Fixed-effects linear probability model. GDP growth (standardised by country): +0.007 (p < 0.001) increase in probability of completing any weekly homework/study. N = 833,970; Countries = 38.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2003/2009/2015/2018 data on homework engagement, the study leveraged GDP growth (standardised by country) together with sex, grade level, tertiary-educated parent status, and reading achievement to predict the probability of completing any weekly homework/study, finding that better economic conditions are associated with higher homework engagement (+0.007 probability per 1 SD GDP growth; p < 0.001). This indicates that economic downturns may reduce students’ study effort, suggesting that schools and support programs should target homework and learning-time continuity during hard times.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Fixed-effects linear probability model. GDP growth (standardised by country): +0.008 (p < 0.001) increase in probability of completing 10+ hours weekly homework/study. N = 833,970; Countries = 38.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2003/2009/2015/2018 data on high-intensity homework engagement, the study leveraged GDP growth (standardised by country) alongside sex, grade level, tertiary-educated parent status, and reading achievement to predict the probability of completing 10+ hours weekly homework/study, finding that students are more likely to do above-average homework during economic expansions (+0.008 probability per 1 SD GDP growth; p < 0.001). This indicates that macroeconomic conditions can translate into measurable changes in learning time, implying that expectation-support and learning-time interventions may be especially important when GDP growth is weak.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Fixed-effects linear probability model. GDP growth (standardised by country): +0.027 (p < 0.001) increase in probability of completing any out-of-school academic lessons/tutoring. N = 733,596; Countries = 38.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2003/2009/2015/2018 data on participation in out-of-school academic lessons, the study leveraged GDP growth (standardised by country) with sex, grade level, tertiary-educated parent status, and reading achievement to predict tutoring participation, finding that economic expansions increase tutoring engagement (+0.027 probability per 1 SD GDP growth; p < 0.001). This indicates that downturns may reduce access to or participation in supplementary learning, suggesting that targeted tutoring support could help buffer students’ learning opportunities during recessions.

main_findings.target_variable: Arrived late to school in last two weeks (binary)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Fixed-effects linear probability model. GDP growth (standardised by country): −0.010 (p < 0.05) change in probability of arriving late to school. N = 1,203,932; Countries = 38.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2003/2009/2015/2018 data on attendance punctuality, the study leveraged GDP growth (standardised by country) together with sex, grade level, tertiary-educated parent status, and reading achievement to predict arriving late, finding that higher GDP growth is associated with lower lateness (−0.010 probability per 1 SD GDP growth; p < 0.05). This indicates that economic conditions affect not only study effort but also day-to-day school attendance behaviours, implying that schools may need attendance-support strategies during periods of weak economic growth.

data.outcome_summary: This study uses PISA microdata for students aged 15–16 from 38 OECD countries across four waves (2003, 2009, 2015, 2018), merged with OECD macroeconomic data on real GDP growth (from the year prior to PISA administration). It estimates within-country fixed-effects regressions with year fixed effects and school-clustered standard errors, using educational expectations converted to expected years of schooling as the main outcome, plus binary indicators for homework, tutoring, and arriving late. The key results show that higher GDP growth is associated with higher educational expectations (e.g., +0.191 expected years per 1 SD higher standardised GDP growth; quintile 5 vs quintile 1: +0.388 years) and that expected returns to education strengthen in expanding economies (interaction term = 0.712, p < 0.001). The paper reports no ML models and does not document a PV-based outcome or a detailed missing-data strategy beyond missing-value indicators, so causal interpretation is limited to associations.
